ety.text: From Middle English so, swo, zuo, swa, swe, from Old English swā, swǣ, swē (“so, as, the same, such, that”), from Proto-West Germanic *swā, from Proto-Germanic *swa, *swē (“so”), from Proto-Indo-European *swē, *swō (reflexive pronomial stem).

chain.g: fifth degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales

ety.text: Shortened from sol, to make it an open syllable for uniformity with the rest of the scale, from Glover's solmization, from Middle English sol (“fifth degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian sol in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin solve (“wash away”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Deacon.
Borrowed from Japanese 蘇 (so).

senses.d: As a result; for that reason; therefore; because of this; due to this.
ex: I was hungry, so I asked if there was any more food.
He ate too much cake and so he fell ill.

senses.d: Used to connect previous conversation or events to the following question.
ex: So how does this story end?

senses.d: Used to introduce a rhetorical question.
ex: “We'd like to visit but I don't know if we can afford a hotel.” — “So who's staying in a hotel? Stay with us.”

senses.d: Provided that; on condition that; as long as.
ex:
Speed. ‘Item: She doth talk in her sleep.’
Launce. It’s no matter for that, so she sleep not in her talk.
As we cal money not onely that which is true and good, but also the false; so it be currant.

senses.d: To the (explicitly stated) extent.
ex: It was so hot outside that all the plants died.
He was so good, they hired him on the spot.

senses.d: To the (implied) extent.
ex: I need a piece of cloth so long. [= this long]

senses.d: Very (positive or negative clause).
ex: I feel so much better now.
I so nearly lost my temper.

senses.d: Very much.
ex: But I so want to see the Queen when she visits our town!
I so wanted to be Jess Harley again.

senses.d: at all (negative clause).
ex: That is so not true!

senses.d: In the same manner or to the same extent as aforementioned; likewise, also.
ex: As above, so below.
He wants to eat now. So does she.

senses.d: Indeed.
ex: ‘Look, it’s just stopped raining.’ ‘So it has!’
‘There are two more.’ ‘So there are.’

senses.d: To such an extent or degree; as.
ex: so far as;  so long as;  so much as

senses.d: Agreeing with actual facts or reality; true.
ex: That is so.
You are responsible for this, is that not so?

senses.d: In that state or manner; with that attribute. A proadjective that replaces the aforementioned adjective phrase.
ex: "You're definitely not right about that." "I am so!" (→I am right about that).
If this separation was painful to all parties, it was most so to Martha.

senses.d: Homosexual.
ex: Is he so?

senses.d: Used after a pause for thought to introduce a new topic, question or story, or a new thought or question in continuation of an existing topic.
ex: So, let's go home.
So, what'll you have?

senses.d: Used as a question to ask for further explanation of something said, often rhetorically or in a dismissive or impolite manner.
ex: "You park your car in front of my house every morning." — "So?"

senses.d: Used as a meaningless filler word to begin a response to a question.
ex: What are you doing? / So I'm just fixing this shelf.
What time does the train leave? / So it leaves at 10 o'clock.

senses.d: Be as you are; stand still; used especially to cows; also used by sailors.
That which was previously mentioned; that.
ex: I'll become a loyal friend and remain so.
If that's what you really mean, then just say so.

senses.d: A syllable used in solfège to represent the fifth note of a major scale.
Sometimes syllable for both the second and the fifth.
A type of dairy product, made especially in Japan between the seventh and tenth centuries, by reducing milk by boiling it.

grp.label: interjection used to introduce a new topic

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French alors, from Old French alors, a leurs, allors, alores, alour, alore, alora (also as enlor, enlora, etc.), from Old French a + lors. Compare Italian allora, Spanish alora, Occitan alara and Catalan aleshores.
Inherited from Old French dunc, from Vulgar Latin dunc, from a crossing of Latin tunc with dum. Compare Italian dunque, Occitan donc and Catalan doncs.
Inherited from Latin ad illam hōram (“at that hour”). Compare French alors, Occitan alara, Spanish alora, and Catalan aleshores. By surface analysis, all' + ora.
From Old Galician-Portuguese enton, from Vulgar Latin *in tunc, from Latin in + tunc (“then”). Displaced collateral form entonce. Compare Spanish entonces.
Compare similar constructions with Italian affinché, Spanish a fin de que and Portuguese a fim de que.

Univerbation of per (“for”) + che (“which”), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin. Compare Neapolitan pecché, Sicilian pirchì, and further Romance parallels such as Sardinian pro chite, French pourquoi, Spanish porque/por qué, Portuguese porque/por que.
Univerbation of a + fin(o) + che. Compare similar constructions with French afin que, Spanish a fin de que and Portuguese a fim de que.
From Middle French tellement, telement, from Old French telement. By surface analysis, tel + -ment. Compare Italian talmente.
Inherited from Middle French vrayement, from Old French veraiement. By surface analysis, vrai + -ment. Compare Italian veramente.
From Old French si, from Latin sic (“so, thus”). Doublet of sic.

chain.g: of such size, of such measure

ety.text: Derived from Latin tantus.
From vera (“true”, feminine singular) + -mente (“-ly”). Compare among others French vraiment.

chain.g: so, so much, to such an extent, to such a degree

ety.text: Inherited from Latin tam.

chain.g: more, the more, in a greater measure, to a greater extent

ety.text: Inherited from Latin magis. Consider also derivative Latin magister, whence English master.
From Old Galician-Portuguese tan, from Latin tam (“so”).

chain.g: as, likewise, in the same way

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French aussi, from Old French ossi, ausi, alsi (“as, in the same way as”), from Vulgar Latin *ale si (“other so, else so”), from Latin alid, aliud (“other, another, any other, else”) + sīc (“so, thus”); probably a calque of Frankish *allswā (“as, likewise, in the same way”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum sīc. By surface analysis, ecco + sì. Closely parallel to Dalmatian coisa, Friulian cussì, Istriot cussèi, Sardinian gósi (bosìe, deàsi, etc.), Venetan cusì. Compare also Catalan així, French ainsi, Portuguese assim, Spanish así, Romanian așa, Sicilian accussì.

Inherited from Middle French ainsi, from Old French ensi, ainsins, probably from Latin ad (“to”) + in (“in”) + sīc (“thus”). Alternatively, from Old French ains + si, but this is less likely, especially for the forms beginning with en-. Compare Catalan així, Italian così, Portuguese assim, Romanian așa, Spanish así.

fr:comme ça.gl: like that/this, that/this way, so, thus

es:así.gl: like this; like that; as such; thus; so; thereby; this way, that way

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish assí, from Late Latin ac sīc. Closely parallel to Portuguese assim, Romanian așa, Aromanian ashi. Compare also Catalan així, French ainsi, Italian così.

pt:assim.gl: this way; like this (in this manner)

ety.text: From earlier assi, from Old Galician-Portuguese assi, from Late Latin ac sīc. Closely parallel to Aromanian ashi, Spanish así, Romanian așa. Compare also Catalan així, French ainsi, Italian così.
alternative form of bien
From Vulgar Latin *pos, from Classical Latin post. Compare English post-, Old Galician-Portuguese pós, Italian poi, Romanian păi, apoi.

es:entonces.gl: then, next, thereupon, at that time, at that point

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish entonce, entonces, from Latin in + *tunce, the latter an archaic form of tunc (“then”). Compare Portuguese então and Romanian atunci.
Modification of pues.
From Latin ad (“to, toward, at”) + ibī (“there”). Compare Galician aí, Spanish ahí.
